extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media students, researchers, and general readers interested in media bias
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and editors on how to report controversies without creating a misleading appearance of balance; identifies when and how to weight, present, or exclude opposing views based on evidence and credibility. Useful for newsroom policy, media-ethics training, and critical consumption of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality to evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "False balance ... is a media bias in which journalists present an issue as being more balanced between opposing viewpoints than the evidence supports.", i.e., do not present issues as more balanced than the evidence warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh and present viewpoints in proportion to the supporting evidence. Anti-pattern: giving equal platform to opposing views when one side is overwhelmingly supported by facts and research. Examples from the page: climate change coverage and MMR vaccine reporting, where giving equal airtime misrepresents consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report credible or reasonable opposing positions with verified facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "news media are responsible for reporting all (credible or reasonable) opposing positions, along with verified facts that may support one or the other side of an issue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include opposing claims that are credible or reasonable; accompany coverage with verified facts that clarify the state of evidence. Guidance implies journalists should vet claims before presenting them as legitimate opposing positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit information that establishes claims as baseless
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journalists may present evidence and arguments out of proportion to the actual evidence for each side, or may omit information that would establish one side's claims as baseless."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid omission of key contextual evidence or rebuttals that would show a position to be unsupported. Scoring note: coverage that omits decisive evidence should be downgraded for misleading balance. Example: media reports that failed to include evidence undermining Wakefield's claims on MMR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving unsupported or dubious positions an illusion of respectability
rubrics_metrics.description: "False balance ... gives unsupported or dubious positions an illusion of respectability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about platforming hypotheses or actors that lack evidence in a way that makes them appear legitimate. Editorial policy should prevent elevating fringe claims through neutral-seeming coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge scientific consensus where it exists
rubrics_metrics.description: "It creates a public perception that some issues are scientifically contentious, although in reality they are not" (e.g., overwhelming scientific consensus on anthropogenic global warming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a clear scientific consensus exists, coverage should make that consensus explicit and avoid framing the story as an unresolved debate. Example: explicitly report the consensus on climate change rather than presenting deniers as equally supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight viewpoints according to merit and significance rather than equal time
rubrics_metrics.description: "Producers and editors may consider treating competing viewpoints fairly—in proportion to their actual merits and significance—as equivalent to treating them equally, giving them equal time... even though one of the viewpoints may be overwhelmingly dominant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness does not mean equal airtime; allocate attention according to evidentiary merit and public significance. Anti-pattern: giving fringe views equal time under the pretense of neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate major and minor positions or present minor issues as equal in weight
rubrics_metrics.description: "Media would then present two opposing viewpoints on an issue as equally credible, or present a major issue on one side of a debate as having the same weight as a minor one on the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish major, well-supported positions from minor or fringe ones; assign prominence and credibility accordingly. Example: avoid treating a widely supported scientific finding and a marginal dissent as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism that frames accurate accounts as contentious for commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: "False balance can also originate from... sensationalism, where producers and editors may feel that a story portrayed as a contentious debate would be more commercially successful than a more accurate (or widely-agreed) account of the issue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manufacture or overstate controversy for ratings or clicks. Editorial incentives should not drive framing that misrepresents the state of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to viewpoint discrimination and political bias as causes of false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: "False balance can be the result of viewpoint discrimination or political bias. Political bias can be evaluated relative to the median voter for particular topics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage choices reflect selective inclusion/exclusion of perspectives for ideological reasons. Review coverage for systematic viewpoint discrimination and evaluate bias relative to a relevant political or social baseline.
